groups.heading: OPTIONAL SOURCE DEPTH
items: British India treated Afghanistan, Burma, Nepal, Tibet, Sikkim and Bhutan not as
distant foreign-policy questions but as security extensions of the Indian empire.
The north-west frontier was dominated by fear of Russia, known as the Great Game , and by the debate between close-border and forward policies.
The First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42) showed the danger of aggressive intervention

groups.heading: ADVANCED DEBATE
items: the Second Anglo-Afghan War (1878–80) produced the Treaty of Gandamak and reinforced British control over Afghan external relations.
CAUTION: The frontier was both a military zone and an ideological zone where imperial rulers claimed to defend India by controlling neighbours.
Burma was conquered in stages through three wars
after the Third Anglo-Burmese War (1885), Upper Burma was annexed and Burma remained tied administratively to India until 1937.

groups.heading: LEGACY / NUANCE
items: Nepal was not annexed after the Treaty of Sagauli; it became a buffer with a Residency and a source of Gurkha recruitment.
Tibet drew Curzon's attention because of fears about Russian influence; the Younghusband Mission of 1904 reflected forward frontier activism.
CAUTION: These policies left boundary legacies, strategic habits and frontier zones that continued to matter after independence.
First Anglo-Afghan War (1839–42) is associated with Auckland and the disastrous Kabul retreat.
